summary: Describes a method for compressing IPX datagram headers over wide area links, so less bandwidth goes to overhead. It is now historic.

eli5.summary: A long address on every envelope wastes space. This memo shows how to shorten the repeating parts so more room is left for real messages.

questions: how does ipx header compression work
subtitle: A Van Jacobson style trick that shrinks 30-byte IPX headers down to one to seven bytes on slow links.

tldr.problem: On slow wide area links every byte counts, and each IPX packet carries a 30 octet header whose fields mostly repeat from packet to packet.
tldr.mechanism: CIPX keeps a copy of each connection's full header in a numbered slot at both ends, then sends a one-octet flags field plus only the fields that changed. A confirmed exchange of an Initial packet sets the slot up.
tldr.outcome: For normal IPX traffic the RFC claims about 2:1 compression including header and data. The RFC is now Historic.

today: RFC 1553 is Historic. The unit metadata lists no replacement RFC. It was a Standards Track document from December 1993 and works with RFC 1552 (IPXCP) for negotiation on PPP links.

sections.title: Why Compress IPX Headers
sections.content:
IPX (Internetwork Packet Exchange) is a Novell protocol derived from XNS's Internet Datagram Protocol. It is connectionless, needs no acknowledgment per packet, and corresponds to the network layer. An IPX packet has a 30 octet header, usually followed by a transport header: 6 octets for the NetWare Core Protocol (NCP) or 12 octets for SPX.

RFC 1553 describes two header compression strategies based on those Van Jacobson described for TCP/IP. One compresses only the IPX header, from 30 octets to between one and seven. The other compresses the combined 36 octet NCP/IPX header, to between one and eight octets. Implementations of CIPX must support both. Header compression can also be combined with data compression, but data compression MUST be done after header compression when sending, and data decompression MUST be done before header decompression when receiving.
sections.eli5: Slow phone lines make big envelope labels expensive. CIPX is a way to use much shorter labels for packets that keep going to the same place.

sections.title: What Can Be Left Out
sections.content:
The RFC goes through the IPX header field by field. The Checksum is normally 0xFFFF, so it can be dropped, but a real checksum MUST be included. Packet Length can usually be worked out from the link layer, but it must be included when the link cannot tell (for example, when hardware pads packets). The Hops, Packet Type and the 12-octet destination and source addresses (network 4, node 6, socket 2) stay constant for a connection. So only Checksum and Length may need to be sent.

For NCP packets, only types 0x2222 (request) and 0x3333 (reply) get NCP compression. The sequence number can be inferred because it rises by one per request, and the connection number is constant. The task number can change, so it is sent when it differs from the last one. Burst Mode packets (type 0x7777) have a 36 octet burst header and are not NCP-compressed, but their IPX header still can be. The RFC does not describe a similar mechanism for SPX.
sections.eli5: Most of the label never changes during a conversation, so you only need to send the parts that do change, like the size of the message.

sections.title: The CIPX Flags Octet and Packet Types
sections.content:
Once compression is negotiated, every IPX packet on the link starts with a CIPX header of at least one octet, even a regular packet. The low bits of the Flags octet give the packet type: 0 Compressed, 1 Regular, 3 Confirmed Initial, 5 Confirm, 7 Unconfirmed Initial, 9 Reject, and 11 to 15 reserved. Only Compressed packets have a lowest bit of zero. The Flags octet MUST NOT be 0xFF, so a normal IPX header with a 0xFFFF checksum is never mistaken for a CIPX one.

In a Compressed packet the four high flag bits say whether the following fields are present, in order: slot number, checksum (2 octets), length (1 to 3 octets) and NCP task number. A flag of 0 means assume the same slot as last time, the checksum 0xFFFF, the length from the link layer, or the same task number. The smallest compressed header is the flags octet alone (0x00), and the largest is 7 octets, or 8 with the task number.

The length field is variable. Values 0 to 127 take one octet. Values 128 to 16383 take two, with the first octet in the range 128 to 191. Larger values use a first octet of 192 followed by two more octets.
sections.eli5: Each packet starts with a small tag saying what kind it is and which extras follow. A tag of zero extras means a super short packet.

sections.title: Slots, Initial Packets and Confirmation
sections.content:
Both ends keep tables of slots, typically one per client-server connection, each holding a full copy of the original IPX header. The compressor compares against it to find changed fields. The decompressor uses it to rebuild the header.

A Confirmed Initial packet (type 3) carries a full IPX packet plus a slot number and a one-octet ID, and asks for confirmation. The decompressor answers with a Confirm packet (type 5) of exactly 3 octets: flags, slot and ID. Only then does the compressor start sending Compressed packets. An Unconfirmed Initial packet (type 7) installs a header without asking for confirmation, so compressed packets can follow at once. A Regular packet (type 1) carries uncompressed IPX, for example when memory for a new slot is short.

A Reject packet (type 9, 3 octets) tells the compressor that a packet used a header the receiver does not support. This is meant to regulate future extensions. Confirmation matters because if an Initial packet is lost, later compressed packets cannot be decompressed correctly.
sections.eli5: First you send the full address and ask, did you get it? Once the other side says yes, you can use the short number. If you do not care about a reply, you can skip asking and just start.

sections.title: Negotiating CIPX over PPP and IPXWAN
sections.content:
Over PPP, CIPX is negotiated with the IPX-Compression-Protocol option of IPXCP (RFC 1552), using protocol value 0002 (hex) for Telebit compressed IPX. The option is 6 octets long and adds Max-Slot-Id (one less than the number of slots) and an Options octet. Option value 1 allows the slot identifier to be compressed, and 2 redefines Compressed packet type bits 1 to 3 for future use. Each end asks separately if it wants compression in both directions. Compression is off by default.

Over IPXWAN, the option is carried in the Timer Request and Response with option number 80 and data bytes for the CIPX type (00), the options and the number of slots. The response MUST contain a subset of the options requested, and the negotiated slot count is the lower of the two requests. IPXWAN sets up a symmetrical link, so both directions use the same slots and options. Implementations MUST support CIPX without any options.
sections.eli5: Before using short labels, both computers have to agree they will, and how many numbered boxes they will keep. They can do this with either of two Novell-style handshakes.

sections.title: Expected Compression Ratio
sections.content:
The RFC gives a formula: ratio equals (average data length + 30) divided by (average data length + average compressed header length). Performance is better when the slot count exceeds the number of active connections and when packets are small.

With the maximum 546 data octets and a 6 octet header, the ratio is about 1.04. With 1 data octet and a 1 octet header it is 15.50. A likely case of 26 data octets and a 2 octet header gives 2.00, matching the abstract's claim of approximately 2:1. The Security Considerations section says IPX's security features apply fully to CIPX and CIPX does not significantly alter the basic security of IPX.
sections.eli5: Small messages gain the most from shorter labels. A big message barely changes, but a tiny one can shrink a lot.
